title: Transference
hookLine: a fire drill for the last moment: the Tibetan practice of sending the mind up into light
tomorrow: what if all you can manage at the end is one name?

lines: CAN YOU PRACTICE FOR THE END?
cards: Schools run fire drills on calm, sunny days, when nothing is burning. Pilots practice engine failures in simulators, over and over, so their hands know what to do when there's no time to think. Nobody calls that gloomy.
It's how you stay calm when it counts. So if the last moment of a life matters, can you practice for it? Tibetan Buddhism says you can, and it has a name for the drill.
It isn't a breathing exercise or a prayer for later. It's a practice of light.

teach.b: The practice is called phowa, a Tibetan word usually translated as transference. Tibetan teachers describe it this way.

At the moment of death, the practitioner sends their awareness up through the body, out through the crown of the head, into the heart of a Buddha visualized above them, often Amitabha, the Buddha of boundless light.
The awareness itself is often pictured as a small point of light, rising like a spark from a fire. Phowa is listed among the six yogas of Naropa, a set of advanced practices in Tibetan lineages.
And here's the part that matters for anyone curious.
Tradition says phowa is taught by a qualified teacher, in person, usually in retreat, and practiced long before it's ever needed.
That's the fire drill: you rehearse while you're healthy, so that at the end the mind knows the way.

Teachers also describe doing phowa on behalf of someone who is dying, and the Tibetan texts read aloud near the dead return again and again to light: recognize the light, go toward it, don't be afraid of it.
None of that can be learned from a short lesson, and this isn't phowa.
But one piece of it is open to anyone.
The picture of light above you, warm and kind, and a mind that leans toward it.

how: In Tibetan Buddhism, phowa is taught by a qualified lama, often in group retreats, and practiced over many sessions; lamas and practitioners may also perform phowa for a person who is dying or has just died.

games.why: phowa is passed on by teachers, in person. the simple picture of light above you is the piece anyone can hold.

practice: Sit tall and close your eyes. Picture a soft light a little above your head, warm like late sun through a window, kind rather than bright.

With each breath in, feel your attention lift gently toward it, and with each breath out, let your shoulders settle. If the picture fades, just feel the top of your head, and lean toward the light again.

wordCard.voice: Phowa: transference. A Tibetan practice, taught by teachers, for sending the mind toward light at the moment of death, rehearsed long before, leaning toward a Buddha's light.

orig.note: Tibetan 'pho ba: transference, changing place; written phowa in English.

carryVoice: Line for today: toward the light, a drill practiced on sunny days. Twenty-four of thirty, done.
